question_text: A 60-year-old man comes to the office because of an 8-month history of cough, night sweats, shortness of breath, and fatigue. He has also had a 9-kg (19.8-lb) weight loss during this time. He appears pale. Abdominal examination shows hepatosplenomegaly. His leukocyte count is 80,000/mm3 and his leukocyte alkaline phosphatase level is increased. A peripheral blood smear shows > 82% neutrophils with band forms and immature and mature neutrophil precursors. An x-ray of the chest shows a 9-mm right hilar nodule. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's laboratory findings?

                    ### Question
                    A 60-year-old man comes to the office because of an 8-month history of cough, night sweats, shortness of breath, and fatigue. He has also had a 9-kg (19.8-lb) weight loss during this time. He appears pale. Abdominal examination shows hepatosplenomegaly. His leukocyte count is 80,000/mm3 and his leukocyte alkaline phosphatase level is increased. A peripheral blood smear shows > 82% neutrophils with band forms and immature and mature neutrophil precursors. An x-ray of the chest shows a 9-mm right hilar nodule. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's laboratory findings?

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The 60-year-old man presents with cough, night sweats, weight loss, fatigue, leukocytosis (80,000/mm3), increased leukocyte alkaline phosphatase, and a right hilar nodule. These findings suggest a significant hematologic process or malignancy. The leukocytosis with immature neutrophil forms and high leukocyte alkaline phosphatase level indicates a possible leukemoid reaction, which can occur in response to severe infections or malignancies. The presence of night sweats and weight loss raises suspicion for chronic infections like tuberculosis, but the leukocytosis and peripheral blood smear findings are more indicative of a myeloproliferative disorder. Given the age of the patient and the laboratory findings, chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is a strong possibility, as it typically presents with leukocytosis and can be associated with splenomegaly. The right hilar nodule may also suggest a secondary process related to malignancy. Therefore, the most likely cause of this patient's laboratory findings is chronic myeloid leukemia.
